statement: Gilgamesh Tablet XI's flood story is a later literary reworking of the older Atraḫasīs flood tradition; scholarship treats Atraḫasīs as the source for the flood section incorporated into the later Gilgamesh epic.

sources.citation: Jeffrey H. Tigay, The Evolution of the Gilgamesh Epic (University of Pennsylvania Press, 1982; reprint 2002), pp. 214–240.
sources.author: Jeffrey H. Tigay
sources.access_note: A scholarly dissertation citing Tigay reproduces his conclusion that Atraḫasīs served as the source for Tablet XI and summarizes the textual reasons.

sources.citation: Andrew R. George, The Babylonian Gilgamesh Epic: Introduction, Critical Edition and Cuneiform Texts (Oxford University Press, 2003), discussion of Tablet XI and the older Atraḫasīs flood tradition.
sources.author: Andrew R. George
sources.access_note: Academic reference summaries based on George's critical edition describe the Tablet XI flood as imported from the older Atraḫasīs tradition.

sources.citation: A. R. George and F. N. H. Al-Rawi, “Tablets from the Sippar Library VI. Atra-ḫasīs,” Iraq 58 (1996): 147–190.
sources.author: Andrew R. George; F. N. H. Al-Rawi
sources.access_note: Peer-reviewed Atraḫasīs study establishing the older epic and its flood narrative context.

does_not_demonstrate: The exact intermediary manuscript history between the Old Babylonian Atraḫasīs tradition and the standard Gilgamesh version is not fully recoverable.
adversarial_counter: The main uncertainty concerns intermediate textual stages, not whether the Gilgamesh flood section derives from the older Atraḫasīs tradition.
